passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Ὁμολογῶ, οὐ συνῆκα πῶς λέγεις „τὰ τῶν ἐπισταμένων ἂν ἐποίεις“. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Εἰ οὐ συνῆκας: οὐδὲ τὸν ἑκάστου νοῦν εἰδέναι δύνῃ — καὶ εἰ ἀγνοεῖς: οὐδὲ τοὺς ἀξίους τῆς ἀποκαλύψεως ἐπίστασαι· εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐπίστασαι, οὐκ εἶ υἱός· ὁ δὲ υἱὸς οἶδεν· διὸ οἷς βούλεται ὡς ἀξίοις οὖσιν ἀποκαλύπτει. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Μὴ ἀπατῶ· οἶδα τοὺς ἀξίους καὶ υἱὸς οὐκ εἰμί. τοῦτο μέντοι τί ποτ’ ἔστιν „οἷς βούλεται ἀποκαλύπτει“, οὐ συνῆκα ὡς λέγεις· τὸ δὲ μὴ συνιέναι οὐχ ὡς μὴ εἰδὼς εἶπον, ἀλλ’ ὡς εἰδὼς ὅτι οἱ παρεστῶτες οὐ συνῆκαν, ἵνα αὐτὸ σαφέστερον εἴπῃς, ὅπως νοήσωσιν ὧν ἕνεκεν καὶ τὴν ζήτησιν ποιούμεθα. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἐγὼ σαφέστερον αὐτὸ εἰπεῖν οὐ δύναμαι, σὺ αὐτὸς ὡς νοήσας φράσον. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἐγὼ τὰ σὰ οὐκ ἀνάγκην ἔχω λέγειν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Φαίνῃ μοι, Σίμων, μὴ συνιεὶς αὐτὸ καὶ ὁμολογεῖν μὴ θέλων, ἵνα μὴ ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ φωραθεὶς ἐλεγχθῇς μὴ ὢν σὺ ὁ ἑστὼς υἱός. τοῦτο γὰρ αἰνίσσῃ, κἂν σαφῶς αὐτὸ εἰπεῖν μὴ θέλῃς· ὥστε ἐγὼ μὲν τὰς σὰς βουλὰς ἐξ ὧν αἰνίσσῃ ἐπίσταμαι, προφήτου ἀληθοῦς μαθητὴς ὤν, οὐ προφήτης. σὺ δὲ καὶ τὰ σαφῶς λεγόμενα μὴ συνιὼν υἱὸν ἑαυτὸν εἰπεῖν θέλεις, ἀνθεστὼς ἡμῖν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἀρῶ σου πᾶσαν πρόφασιν· ὁμολογῶ, αὐτὸ οὐ συνῆκα τί ποτ’ ἔστιν „καὶ οἷς ἂν βούληται ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύπτει“. λέγε τοίνυν αὐτὸ σαφέστερον.

τοῦτο τοῦ Πέτρου εἰπόντος ἀπὸ μὲν τῶν ὄχλων ἔπαινος ἐγένετο. ὁ δὲ Σίμων κατάφωρος γεγονώς, αἰδεσθεὶς ἠρυθρίασεν καὶ τὸ μέτωπον τρίψας ἔφη Ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ μάγον λέγουσιν ὑπὸ Πέτρου νικώμενον, ἀλλὰ καὶ συλλογιζόμενον. οὐκ εἴ τις δὲ συλλογισθείη, συναρπασθεὶς τὴν ἐν·αὐτῷ ἀλήθειαν νενικημένην ἔχει· οὐ γὰρ ἡ ἀσθένεια τοῦ ἐκδικοῦντος ἀλήθειά ἐστιν τοῦ νικωμένου. πλὴν φημί σοι ὅτι ἐγὼ τοὺς παρεστῶτας πάντας ἀξίους ἔκρινα γνῶναι τὸν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις πατέρα. διὸ δημοσίᾳ μου αὐτοῖς ἀποκαλύπτοντος, οὐ αὐτοῖς διὰ φθόνον ἐμοὶ τῷ εὐεργετεῖν αὐτοὺς θέλοντι χαλεπαίνειν.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ἐπειδὴ ἀρεσκόντως τοῖς παροῦσιν ὄχλοις οὕτως ἔφης, ἐγὼ ἐρῶ οὐκ ἀρεσκόντως, ἀλλὰ ἀληθῶς. λέγε μοι, πῶς ἀξίους ἐπίστασαι τοὺς παρεστῶτας πάντας, ὅπου σοι ἐκφαίνοντι οὐδὲ εἷς συνέθετο; τὸ γὰρ ἐμοὶ ποιήσασθαι κατὰ σοῦ τὸν ἔπαινον οὐκ ἔστιν συγκαταθεμένων σοί, ἀλλὰ ἐμοί, ᾧ καὶ τὸν ἔπαινον ὡς ὀρθῶς εἰρηκότι ἀπένειμαν. ἀλλ’ ἐπειδὴ ὁ θεὸς δίκαιος ὢν βραβεύει τὸν ἑκάστου νοῦν, ὃ φῆς ἀληθὲς εἶναι, οὐκ ἂν ἐβουλήθη διὰ τῆς ἀριστερᾶς τοῖς δεξιοῖς τοῦτο δοθῆναι, ᾧ λόγῳ ὁ παρὰ κλέπτου τι λαβὼν καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπεύθυνός ἐστιν. ὥστε τούτου ἕνεκεν τὸ ὑπὸ σοῦ φερόμενον οὐκ ἠθέλησεν αὐτοὺς λαβεῖν, ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦ εἰς τὸ ἀποκαλύπτειν ὡρισμένου υἱοῦ. τίνι γὰρ εὔλογόν ἐστιν ἀποκαλύπτειν τὸν πατέρα ἢ υἱῷ μόνῳ διὰ τὸ εἰδέναι τῆς τοιαύτης ἀποκαλύψεως τὸν ἄξιον; οὕτως οὐκ ἔστιν·τοῦτο διδάξαι ἢ διδαχθῆναι, ἀλλ’ ἀφράστῳ χειρὶ ἀποκαλυφθῆναι τῷ τοῦτο εἰδέναι ἀξίῳ.

ἡμεῖς, ὦ Σίμων, ἐκ τῆς μεγάλης δυνάμεως, ἔτι τε καὶ τῆς κυρίας λεγομένης, οὐ λέγομεν δύο ἀπεστάλθαι ἀγγέλους, τὸν μὲν ἐπὶ τῷ κτίσαι κόσμον, τὸν δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ θέσθαι τὸν νόμον — οὐδ’ ὅτι ἑαυτὸν ἕκαστος, ἐλθὼν ἐφ’ οἷς ἐποίησεν ὡς αὐτὸς ὢν αὐθέντης, αὐτὸς ἤγγειλεν — οὐδὲ ὁ ἑστὼς στησόμενος ἀντικείμενος. μάθε πῶς ἀπιστεῖς καὶ τὴν ὑπόθεσιν ταύτην. ἣν φῄς δύναμιν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις εἶναι, ἀγνοίας γέμει· τὴν γὰρ ἀγνωμοσύνην τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ἀποσταλέντων ἀγγέλων οὐ προεγίνωσκεν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων τοῦ Πέτρου ταῦτα λέγοντος μεγάλως ὀργισθεὶς ἐπέκοψεν λέγοντα, εἰπὼν Τί φλυαρεῖς, τολμηρὲ καὶ πάντων προπετέστατε, ἐπ’ ὄχλων ἀμαθῶν ἐκφαίνων ἀτέχνως τὰ ἀπόρρητα; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Τί φθονεῖς εὐεργετεῖσθαι τοὺς παρόντας ἀκροατάς; καὶ ὁ Σίμων Οὐκοῦν ὁμολογεῖς τὴν τοιαύτην ἐπίγνωσιν εὐεργεσίαν εἶναι; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ὁμολογῶ· τὸ γὰρ ψεῦδος γνωσθὲν εὐεργετεῖ ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ μὴ περιπεσεῖν αὐτῷ. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Φαίνῃ μοι μὴ δυνάμενος εἰπεῖν εἰς ἃ προέτεινά σοι. λέγω δὲ ὅτι καὶ ὁ διδάσκαλός σου ἐν ἀπορρήτοις τινὰ λέγει εἶναι πατέρα.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ἀποκρινοῦμαι εἰς ὃ θέλεις, περὶ „τοῦ οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα, εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός — οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις οἶδεν, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατὴρ καὶ οἷς ἂν βούληται ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψαι“. πρῶτον μὲν θαυμάζω πῶς τοῦ λόγου τούτου μυρίας ἔχοντος ἐκδοχὰς σὺ τὸ ἐπικινδυνότερον ἐξελέξω μέρος, πρὸς ἀγνωσίαν τοῦ δημιουργοῦ καὶ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ πάντων φήσας εἰρῆσθαι τὸν λόγον. πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ δύναται ὁ λόγος εἰρῆσθαι πρὸς πάντας Ἰουδαίους, τοὺς πατέρα νομίζοντας εἶναι χριστοῦ τὸν Δαυὶδ — καὶ αὐτὸν δὲ τὸν χριστὸν υἱὸν ὄντα — καὶ υἱὸν θεοῦ μὴ ἐγνωκέναι. διὸ καὶ οἰκείως εἴρηται „οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα“, ἐπεὶ ἀντὶ τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν Δαυὶδ πάντες ἔλεγον. τὸ δὲ ἐπάξαντα εἰπεῖν ὡς „οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις οἶδεν“: ἐπεὶ αὐτὸν υἱὸν ὄντα οὐκ ᾔδεισαν. καὶ τὸ εἰπεῖν „οἷς ἂν βούληται ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψαι“ ὀρθῶς εἴρηται· ὁ γὰρ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ὢν υἱὸς μόνος ὡρίσθη, ἵνα οἷς βούλεται ἀποκαλύψῃ. καὶ οὕτως δύναται Ἀδὰμ ὁ πρωτόπλαστος αὐτὸν μὴ ἀγνοεῖν οὐδὲ Ἐνὼχ ὁ εὐαρεστήσας μὴ εἰδέναι οὔτε Νῶε ὁ δίκαιος μὴ ἐπίστασθαι οὔτε Ἀβραὰμ ὁ φίλος μὴ συνιέναι, οὐχ Ἰσαὰκ μὴ νενοηκέναι, οὐχ Ἰακὼβ ὁ παλαίσας μὴ πεπιστευκέναι, καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐν τῷ λαῷ ἀξίοις μὴ ἀποκεκαλύφθαι.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: Simon said, “I admit I did not understand how you mean, ‘You would do the things done by those who know.’” Peter said, “If you did not understand, you also cannot know each person’s mind. And if you do not know, you also do not know those worthy of revelation. If you do not know, you are not Son; but the Son knows, and therefore reveals to those he wishes as being worthy.” Simon said, “Let me not deceive: I know those who are worthy, and I am not Son. Yet I did not understand what this is, ‘He reveals to those he wishes,’ as you say. I said that I did not understand not because I did not know, but because I knew that those present did not understand, so that you would state it more clearly and those for whose sake we also conduct the discussion might understand.” Peter said, “I cannot state it more clearly. Since you have understood it, explain it yourself.” Simon said, “I am not obliged to state your views.” Peter said, “It seems to me, Simon, that you do not understand it and are unwilling to admit it, lest, being caught in ignorance, you be exposed as not being the standing Son. For this is what you hint at, even if you do not wish to say it plainly. Thus I know your intentions from your hints, being a disciple of a true prophet, not a prophet. But you, though you do not understand even what is plainly said, wish to call yourself Son, standing against us.” Simon said, “I will remove every excuse from you. I admit that I did not understand what this is: ‘And to those to whom the Son wishes, he reveals.’ So state it more clearly.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the epithet tied to Simon’s alleged claim; it is not identified with an external historical person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προφήτου ἀληθοῦς μαθητὴς ὤν, οὐ προφήτης
lexical_decisions.chosen: being a disciple of a true prophet, not a prophet
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves Peter’s explicit denial of being a prophet in this statement, rather than harmonizing it to a later title.

ἀπατῶ is first-person singular, compatible with a first-person subjunctive here; let me not deceive preserves that person and the negative. The possible interrogative indicative alternative is Am I deceiving?, expecting a negative answer. The edition’s printed stop fits the chosen noninterrogative construction, but does not settle the form’s mood. No second-person imperative or replacement Greek is introduced.

passages.text: After Peter said this, praise arose from the crowds. Simon, thoroughly exposed, blushed in shame, rubbed his forehead, and said, “But they call me a magician, defeated by Peter, and also caught in argument. Yet if someone is caught in argument and taken unawares, he does not thereby have the truth within him defeated; for the weakness of its defender is not the truth of the defeated party. Nevertheless I tell you that I judged everyone present worthy to know the Father who is in secret. Therefore, when I reveal him to them publicly, they should not be angry with me out of envy, since I wish to do them good.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The form can mean reasoning or being brought under a syllogistic argument. The context of defeat and being taken unawares favors being caught in argument; reasoning is a material alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἡ ἀσθένεια τοῦ ἐκδικοῦντος ἀλήθειά ἐστιν τοῦ νικωμένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: the weakness of its defender is not the truth of the defeated party
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the compact distinction between a weak defender and the truth he defends rather than rewriting it as truth’s weakness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ αὐτοῖς διὰ φθόνον ἐμοὶ τῷ εὐεργετεῖν αὐτοὺς θέλοντι χαλεπαίνειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they should not be angry with me out of envy, since I wish to do them good
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes αὐτοῖς as the persons for whom getting angry is inappropriate, leaving the grammatical third-person reference intact instead of silently changing it to you, Peter.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to know the Father who is in secret
lexical_decisions.rationale: The secrecy phrase describes the Father, not a secret manner of knowing. This distinction fits Simon’s immediately following public disclosure and agrees with the attributive rendering in 18.6.

passages.text: Peter said, “Since you have spoken in this way to please the crowds present, I will speak not to please them, but truthfully. Tell me: how do you know that everyone present is worthy, when not even one agreed with you as you disclosed it? For their praising me against you is not the act of people agreeing with you, but with me, to whom they also assigned praise as someone who had spoken rightly. But since God, being just, judges each person’s mind—which you say is true—he would not have wished this to be given to those on the right through the left. By the same reasoning, someone who receives anything from a thief is himself liable. Therefore, for this reason, he did not wish them to receive what you bring, but rather through the Son appointed to reveal. For who can reasonably reveal the Father except the Son alone, since he knows who is worthy of such revelation? Thus this cannot be taught or learned by teaching, but must be revealed by an inexpressible hand to the one worthy to know it.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to those on the right through the left
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the right/left opposition without identifying unprinted named camps or persons.
Retains the hand image, not merely a generic divine act.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνι γὰρ εὔλογόν ἐστιν ἀποκαλύπτειν τὸν πατέρα ἢ υἱῷ μόνῳ διὰ τὸ εἰδέναι τῆς τοιαύτης ἀποκαλύψεως τὸν ἄξιον;
lexical_decisions.chosen: For who can reasonably reveal the Father except the Son alone, since he knows who is worthy of such revelation?
lexical_decisions.rationale: τίνι and υἱῷ identify the person for whom revealing is appropriate, thus the revealer. The Son’s preceding appointment and knowledge of worthy recipients confirm this role. The English does not make him the recipient by saying to whom the Father is revealed.

passages.text: “We, Simon, do not say that two angels were sent from the great power, also called the sovereign power, one to create a world and the other to lay down the law. Nor do we say that each came to the things he had made and announced himself as their original author. Nor do we speak of the standing one who will stand as an adversary. Learn how you disbelieve even this hypothesis. The power you say is in secrecy is full of ignorance, for it did not foreknow the ingratitude of the angels it sent.” While Peter was saying this, Simon became very angry and interrupted him, saying, “Why do you babble, you bold man, most reckless of all, plainly disclosing the secrets before uninstructed crowds?” Peter said, “Why do you begrudge the benefit given to the hearers present?” Simon said, “Then do you acknowledge that such knowledge is a benefit?” Peter said, “I do: for once falsehood is known, it gives the benefit of not falling into it through ignorance.” Simon said, “It seems to me that you cannot answer what I put before you. I mean that your teacher too says that there is a certain Father in secrecy.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς μεγάλης δυνάμεως, ἔτι τε καὶ τῆς κυρίας λεγομένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: the great power, also called the sovereign power
lexical_decisions.rationale: κυρίας can qualify power as sovereign, ruling, or mistress-like; sovereign power gives its authority sense without adding a separate named deity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Nor do we speak of the standing one who will stand as an adversary.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominal clause is extremely compressed. The main rendering carries do we speak from the preceding repeated denial and preserves standing, future standing, and adversary without supplying a named identity. Nor is the standing one going to stand as an adversary is another possible grouping.
ἀτέχνως here means plainly or without qualification, not necessarily in an unskilled manner.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you bold man, most reckless of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both bold and the explicit superlative comparison with all (πάντων), not merely the intensifier utterly.

source_issues.issue: The nominal clause leaves its finite verbal relation implicit. The main text carries the preceding denial of doctrinal assertion forward; a direct nominal assertion, nor is the standing one going to stand as an adversary, is another grouping. Every surviving element remains.

passages.text: Peter said, “I will answer what you want, concerning ‘No one knew the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.’ First, I am amazed how, when this statement has countless interpretations, you chose the more dangerous part, saying that the statement referred to ignorance on the part of the maker and everyone made by him. For in the first place the statement can have been addressed to all the Jews who supposed David to be the Messiah’s father—with the Messiah himself being the son—and had not recognized him as Son of God. Therefore it was appropriately said, ‘No one knew the Father,’ since everyone named David instead of God. He added, ‘Nor does anyone know the Son,’ because they did not know that he was Son. Saying, ‘Those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him,’ was also rightly said, for the Son who has existed from the beginning alone was appointed to reveal to those he wishes. Thus Adam, the first formed, can have been not ignorant of him; nor can Enoch, who pleased him, fail to know; nor can righteous Noah fail to understand; nor can Abraham the friend fail to comprehend; nor can Isaac have failed to understand; nor can Jacob who wrestled have failed to believe; nor can he have remained unrevealed to all the worthy among the people.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you chose the more dangerous part
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the comparative, not the unsupported superlative most dangerous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ἀγνωσίαν τοῦ δημιουργοῦ καὶ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ πάντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: ignorance on the part of the maker and everyone made by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitives are taken as subjective: maker and created ones are ignorant of the secret Father, as in Simon’s argument. Ignorance of the maker is an objective-genitive alternative, but fits the immediately preceding exchange less well.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐν τῷ λαῷ ἀξίοις μὴ ἀποκεκαλύφθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: nor can he have remained unrevealed to all the worthy among the people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The final clause is read under the negative modal scope carried from the preceding οὐχ ... μὴ clauses. Its μὴ is retained in unrevealed and the carried denial in nor can. A clause-local reading, and not to have been revealed, remains possible but is less consonant with the preceding argument.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς πατέρα νομίζοντας εἶναι χριστοῦ τὸν Δαυὶδ — καὶ αὐτὸν δὲ τὸν χριστὸν υἱὸν ὄντα — καὶ υἱὸν θεοῦ μὴ ἐγνωκέναι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: who supposed David to be the Messiah’s father—with the Messiah himself being the son—and had not recognized him as Son of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed parenthesis is kept outside the failure-to-recognize phrase and can continue the supposed Davidic father-son relation. It could instead affirm the Messiah’s sonship parenthetically. A broader attachment, taking their failure as not recognizing him as Son and as Son of God, is a material alternative, but the parenthetical punctuation favors keeping the explicit Son-of-God denial as the failed recognition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲ Ἐνὼχ ὁ εὐαρεστήσας μὴ εἰδέναι οὔτε Νῶε ὁ δίκαιος μὴ ἐπίστασθαι οὔτε Ἀβραὰμ ὁ φίλος μὴ συνιέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: nor can Enoch ... fail to know; nor can righteous Noah fail to understand; nor can Abraham ... fail to comprehend
lexical_decisions.rationale: The governing δύναται is carried through the list, with οὐδέ/οὔτε denying the modal possibility of each negative-infinitive failure. This gives the explicit nor can ... fail construction. Another reading coordinates the negative infinitival complements under a positive possibility—can be not ignorant, can be not without knowledge—without the same emphasis on exclusion of ignorance. The first Adam clause has only the negative infinitive and is kept as a positive possibility of nonignorance; the later coordinated negatives are made explicit rather than flattened.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐν τῷ λαῷ ἀξίοις μὴ ἀποκεκαλύφθαι
source_issues.issue: The final coordination has μὴ but no newly repeated οὐχ. The English carries the previous negative modal scope, nor can ... unrevealed, rather than adding a new printed negation. A clause-local reading would instead yield and not revealed. The modal/negative scope across the entire list is explained in the lexical note on Enoch, Noah, and Abraham.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
